title: The scams get sophisticated
description: Nearly identical domains, urgent PIX transfers, tampered invoices, fake Microsoft alerts, and a compromised vendor. Nothing is what it seems at first glance.

events.message: The store's internet is slow today — every second counts even more.

emails.subject: Access confirmation required
emails.bodyHtml: Dear employee, we detected a new device trying to access your account. Confirm it was you by clicking the link below, or your account will be suspended for security reasons.

internalDbRecord.notes: Domain visually identical to the official one, registered 3 days ago.

investigationHints.summaryText: Look closely: the address uses an uppercase 'I' in place of a lowercase 'l'. It's the swapped-letter trick, which fools the eye.
SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all failed.
Address that looks exactly like the official one, but was created only 3 days ago.

explanation.short: Homograph attack: uppercase 'I' in place of lowercase 'l'.
explanation.detailed: The uppercase letter 'I' looks like a lowercase 'l' in many fonts. This email uses 'leroymerIin.com.br' instead of 'leroymerlin.com.br': it looks the same, but it's a different address, created only 3 days ago. It's the swapped-letter trick.

emails.subject: URGENT: I need you to send a PIX transfer now
emails.bodyHtml: I'm in a meeting with an important vendor and need to close a payment now via PIX so we don't lose the special deal. Confirm with me once you've done it, I'll explain later. Key: 47.xxx.xxx/0001-xx

aiAssistantHint.reasoning: Urgent PIX request, with no formal approval process, coming from an unofficial corporate domain — a classic Business Email Compromise (BEC) pattern.

investigationHints.summaryText: 'leroymerlin-corp.com' is not the company's official address.
The AI identifies a classic PIX/BEC fraud pattern with high confidence.

explanation.short: Fake-payment scam: an urgent PIX pretending to be management.
explanation.detailed: An urgent PIX request, with no approval and using pressure ('I'm in a meeting', 'don't lose the deal'), is the fake-payment scam. The address it came from is not the company's official one. An urgent payment should always be confirmed through another channel before it's made.

emails.subject: Updated payment slip - Constrular Vendor
emails.bodyHtml: Attached is the updated payment slip for the last shipment of materials. Please use only this slip for payment, the previous one was canceled due to a value error.

internalDbRecord.notes: Vendor active for 5 years. Registered payee: 'Constrular Materiais de Construção LTDA'.

investigationHints.summaryText: The registered payee is 'Constrular Materiais de Construção LTDA' — check whether the attached slip matches this name before paying.
The file is technically a legitimate PDF, but that doesn't guarantee the banking details inside it haven't been tampered with.
SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all pass — the originating server really does belong to the vendor.

explanation.short: Real vendor, but payment slip with a tampered payee.
explanation.detailed: This is the most dangerous case: a real sender, a real address, all the email's checks passing. The scam is inside the PDF: the payee on the slip was swapped for a different account. The defense here isn't technical. Always confirm a change of payment details by phone, with a contact you already know at the vendor. Never by email alone.

emails.subject: Microsoft: your Office 365 license expires today
emails.bodyHtml: Your Microsoft 365 license expires today at 11:59pm. Click below to renew automatically and avoid losing access to your files.

investigationHints.summaryText: 'micros0ft-online.com' uses the number zero in place of the letter 'o'. It's not a Microsoft address.
The certificate is technically valid, but issued for the fake domain, not for the real Microsoft.

explanation.short: Fake Microsoft address, with a number in place of a letter.
explanation.detailed: 'micros0ft-online.com' swaps the 'o' for a zero: it's the lookalike-address trick. The site's padlock works, but that only says the connection is secure, not that the site belongs to Microsoft. The real Microsoft would never use this address, and the email's checks failed.

emails.subject: Banking details update - Eletrotech Vendor
emails.bodyHtml: Dear all, due to internal restructuring, our bank account has changed. Please update our records for upcoming payments using the attached details. Thank you for your understanding.

internalDbRecord.notes: Vendor active for 4 years. No formal request for a change in banking details on file.

investigationHints.summaryText: There is no formal request for a banking details change in progress for this vendor.
SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all pass — the email really did come from the vendor's server.

explanation.short: Real vendor account compromised to divert payments.
explanation.detailed: Everything here looks real: a real address, the email's checks passing. The scam is the change of banking details requested by email alone, with no process. It's a sign of a real vendor whose account was hacked. Any change to a vendor's banking details should be confirmed by phone, with a contact you already know. Never just by email.

emails.subject: Monthly operations meeting agenda
emails.bodyHtml: Attached is the agenda for tomorrow's monthly operations meeting, at 10am in the training room. Attendance is mandatory for department leaders.

investigationHints.summaryText: Legitimate PDF, extension and actual type match, no macro.

explanation.short: Legitimate internal announcement with a safe attachment.
explanation.detailed: Official address, the email's checks passing, and the attachment is a genuine PDF with no sign of a virus. Not every attachment is dangerous: what matters is checking before you decide.
